• Other names: Baptist plant, Border plant, Calico plant, Red calico plant, Joyweed, Jacob's coat, Joseph's coat, Parrot leaf
  • Difficulty: difficult
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • pH: 6.0–7.5
  • GH: 1–12
  • Temperature: 24–30°C
  • Substrate: nutrient rich
  • Can be grown emersed: yes
  • Growth rate: low
  • Placement: foreground and midground
  • Height underwater: 10–15 cm
  • CO2 and fertilizers needed
  • Propagation: stem cuttings
  • Colour: green, red, orange

In traditional medicine, Alternanthera bettzickiana is used to promote lactation, for nourishment, as a prophylaxis of dementia and to treat gastrointestinal diseases. It is also used as an antipyretic. Its leaves and shoots are often eaten as vegetables in South East Asia. In Central America it is used as an ant repellent.

The plant's native home was presumably Brazil, from where it escaped and naturalized in the British Virgin Islands, Costa Rica, Colombia, Peru, the Dominican Republic and St. Lucia, and also in Asia (for example China, Thailand, Indonesia, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea) and many other countries. In some countries (such as Papua New Guinea or China) it has spread so extensively that it is considered almost a weed.

Alternanthera bettzickiana thrives in tropical and subtropical regions, commonly found in moist places near ditches, mesh areas or open wastelands. In India, for example, it is found throughout the plains, degraded deciduous forests and wastelands. It occurs from sea level to 2000 m elevation.

The difficulty depends on whether the plant is kept submerged or emersed.

Submerged form

In aquariums it is not recommended for beginners because it has high requirements for light, CO2, nutrients and stable water parameters. It grows extremely slowly even under optimal conditions. In a shallow tank it may reach the water surface, which boosts growth but produces aerial leaves that can overshadow the underwater ones. Monitor water parameters and avoid fluctuations, including temperature changes.

Emersed form

In paludariums the plant becomes fairly hardy and needs little attention. It needs consistently moist but well-drained soil; growth is then moderate to high. In winter it can only survive indoors; even on a south-facing window it may lose its colours and turn green.

Tank size

Grown only as an aquatic plant, it can be kept in nano aquariums, where it will not grow large. Grown emersed, it needs a larger tank of at least 80 litres.

Temperature, hardness and pH

Temperature 24–30°C. The plant is sensitive to sudden temperature fluctuations, which may cause leaf melting. pH 6.0–7.5. Hardness 1–12 GH. Experiments indicate it is not a halophyte; it tolerates moderately saline conditions but growth and survival drop significantly. It is not suitable for brackish tanks.

Lighting

It thrives from full sun to partial shade. Use lighting giving at least medium-high levels (30–50 PAR) with a photoperiod of 10–12 hours daily. It often barely grows if light is insufficient.

Substrate

It prefers organically rich substrates with a depth of at least 5 cm.

CO2 and fertilization

CO2 supplementation is highly recommended; it is very difficult to grow this plant without CO2. High-light plants must be balanced in CO2 and nutrients; strong lighting without CO2 injection leads to algae problems. Liquid fertilizers are required at least a few times a month, otherwise it will not grow. In shrimp tanks, note that high CO2 levels and copper (present in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Propagation

Propagate by stem cuttings:

  • Select a cutting with 4–5 leaves from a healthy stem.
  • Cut it at the nodes.
  • Let it float freely in the water.
  • Once it develops roots, plant it into the substrate 5–8 cm apart.

Alternanthera bettzickiana is a bushy, colourful, ground-covering prostrate perennial herb with green, yellowish and red foliage; leaves can be bicolour or multicoloured. Underwater it grows very slowly and loses its colour variation. Emersed, it can grow over 50 cm tall; fully submerged it barely reaches 15 cm. Stems and branches are hairy when young and become smooth with age. Leaves are opposite, narrow to broadly elliptic, with small hairs on both surfaces, reddish, orange, purple or green. Flowers are creamy white, in clusters, and can appear throughout the year. Seeds are disk-shaped.

Common problems: Temperature – if it drops to 20°C the plant can quickly perish; use a heater if needed. Fragile leaves – some fish (such as Ancistrus) may break them off. Algae – intense light and long photoperiods can trigger algae growth on the leaves; keep CO2, light and fertilizer balanced. Poor growth – usually caused by lack of CO2, low light, low nutrients or a combination. Relocation – once established the root system is extensive and hard to pull out without disturbing other plants.

In conclusion, the plant is challenging underwater, but flourishes in a paludarium.

Etymology: the genus name Alternanthera derives from Latin alternus ("alternate") and Greek anthos, a pollen-bearing part of a flower, likely referring to the alternate arrangement of anthers. The species name honours the German gardener Friedrich Wilhelm August Bettzich (1814–1865).
